fm01_gaikuang.note: Wenshi ziliao xuanji, the serial publication of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference's historical-materials committee, begun in 1960. It solicited first-person accounts from former Nationalist officials, officers and businessmen — many of them, like Shen Zui, recently pardoned prisoners. Almost the whole of this book first appeared there. The series is indispensable and partisan at once: it preserves testimony that exists nowhere else, and it was commissioned, edited and published by the state the witnesses had fought against, in a period when the value of a memoir was measured partly by how thoroughly its author condemned his former self.

Wen Qiang (1907–2001), Shen Zui's colleague in the Juntong and later a Nationalist lieutenant general; captured at the Huai-Hai campaign in 1949, held as a war criminal and pardoned in 1975, the last group released. He was a distant cousin of Mao Zedong on his mother's side. The word "Comrade" here is doing real work: by the time Shen Zui wrote, Wen Qiang had been rehabilitated into the same CPPCC apparatus that published them both.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the Fuxingshe, which some people also called the Blue Shirts
fm01_gaikuang.note: The tangle of names is real and is not the author's confusion. Chinese Renaissance Society (中华复兴社), Vigorous Practice Society (力行社) and Blue Shirts (蓝衣社) were used for overlapping bodies in a concentric structure built around Chiang Kai-shek by Whampoa graduates from 1932. "Blue Shirts" was largely an outsiders' and journalists' name — it circulated widely in the foreign press of the 1930s, which cast the group as China's fascists — and members themselves rarely used it. Historians have argued since the 1980s about how much of the "Blue Shirt" organization existed as described and how much was inferred from hostile reporting; Shen Zui's casual "some people also called it" is closer to the truth than most contemporary accounts.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: Inside the Juntong it was known as the Ten-Man Team.
fm01_gaikuang.note: The founding group of Dai Li's service. Rosters differ between accounts, and even the count is not stable — the phrase means "the original ten" rather than a fixed list, and different memoirists name different men among them. Shen Zui joined later and is reporting the service's own founding legend, which by his day was commemorated annually.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: He Zhonghan, Feng Ti, Teng Jie, Zhou Fu, Kang Ze, Gui Yongqing, Pan Youqiang, Zheng Jiemin and Qiu Kaiji
fm01_gaikuang.note: The Lixingshe's founding council, drawn almost entirely from the Whampoa Military Academy's first class. He Zhonghan and Teng Jie were the principal organizers; Kang Ze ran the propaganda side and the Farmer's Bank militia; Gui Yongqing became a senior field commander. Feng Ti was executed in 1938 for the burning of Changsha, the scorched-earth fire set on a false alarm that destroyed the city and killed thousands — one of the war's worst self-inflicted disasters, for which three officials were shot. That Dai Li appears here only as an alternate member is the point of the paragraph: at the founding he was junior to all of these men, and outlasted nearly all of them.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: The department was established on 1 April 1932.
fm01_gaikuang.note: The date is well attested and the service kept it as its birthday for the rest of its existence — see the "April the First Assembly" below. The Juntong dated itself from the founding of this secret-service department of a semi-secret society, not from the bureau whose name it later carried.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the boss of the CC clique, Chen Lifu
fm01_gaikuang.note: Chen Lifu (1900–2001) and his brother Chen Guofu ran the Kuomintang's party organization and its party-based intelligence service; "CC" is usually explained as the brothers' initials or as "Central Club." The rivalry sketched in this paragraph — party intelligence under the Chens against military intelligence under Dai Li — structures the whole of Nationalist secret-service history, and the 1938 split into Zhongtong and Juntong described further down is its formal settlement.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: his Whampoa class was a late one — the sixth
fm01_gaikuang.note: The Whampoa Military Academy's intake number functioned as a rank of seniority in its own right throughout the Nationalist officer corps, independent of actual position. Dai Li entered with the sixth class in 1926, years behind the first-class men who founded the Lixingshe, and never lost the handicap; the workaround Shen Zui describes — real power as deputy director, the directorship left to a succession of senior figures who did not exercise it — is the standard account of how it was managed.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the Special Political Problems Research Office, run by Zhang Guotao
fm01_gaikuang.note: Zhang Guotao (1897–1979) was a founder of the Chinese Communist Party, present at its first congress in 1921, and commander of the Fourth Front Army; he lost his power struggle with Mao Zedong on the Long March and defected to the Nationalists in April 1938. The Juntong then put him to work against his former party. Nothing else in this chapter's list of offices carries the weight this half-sentence does, and Shen Zui passes over it without comment — a founder of the Communist Party is a line item between a research office and a recreation room. Zhang Guotao later left for Hong Kong and died in Canada. The scan is unambiguous here; the OCR read the name as a nonentity, and it was crop-verified against the page.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: a Zhongshan Room in charge of recreation
fm01_gaikuang.note: Named for Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan). Nationalist units maintained a "Zhongshan Room" as a combined reading room, recreation room and political-instruction space — the Nationalist counterpart to the club rooms of other twentieth-century party-armies.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the aircraft Dai Li was travelling in flew into Dai Hill
fm01_gaikuang.note: Dai Li died on 17 March 1946 when his aircraft, flying from Qingdao to Nanking in bad weather, struck high ground near Banqiao, south-east of the city. The hill is usually given in Chinese sources as 岱山 Dai Hill or the site as Kunyugou; this book prints 戴山, which is the author's own surname-character for Dai Li himself. The homophone has fed a long afterlife of stories about the coincidence of the name. His death is the hinge of the second half of this book: everything about the Bureau of Secrets Preservation, Zheng Jiemin and Mao Renfeng follows from it.

臭招牌, literally "stinking shop-sign." The idiom is ordinary Chinese for a discredited brand, but the register here is not neutral, and it recurs throughout the book: Shen Zui is writing in the early 1960s, as a pardoned war criminal, for a state publication, about an organization he served in for eighteen years. Where the English keeps expressions like this one, or "criminal activities" and "the reactionaries" below, it is preserving evidence of the conditions the book was written under rather than importing a judgement of its own.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: the first thing I did was to confess my guilt to him
fm02_qianyan.note: 请罪, literally "to beg punishment." Shen Zui had been captured in Yunnan in 1949 and held for eleven years; he was released in the first special amnesty of December 1959, which freed thirty-three war criminals judged to have reformed. The reception described here comes fourteen months later. The confession-first reflex is not a literary flourish: it is the trained posture of a man whose release was conditional on having demonstrated exactly that reflex, and it shapes the whole book.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: Vice-Premiers Chen Yi and Luo Ruiqing
fm02_qianyan.note: Chen Yi (1901–1972), marshal, foreign minister and one of the Communist commanders in the very campaigns that ended Shen Zui's career. Luo Ruiqing (1906–1978) was Minister of Public Security from 1949 to 1959 and by 1961 chief of the general staff: that is, the man who had run the apparatus that held Shen Zui was now in the room receiving him. Neither point is made in the text, and both would be obvious to the book's Chinese readers.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: we had merely served as his unpaid escort
fm02_qianyan.note: 义务随从. The joke lands harder in Chinese, where 义务 means "voluntary, unpaid" in the specific sense used of public-spirited service — Zhou is saying the Juntong's surveillance amounted to a free bodyguard detail. This is the anecdote's governing tone: the Premier is not accusing the man in front of him, he is telling him he was never any good at his job.

The Sun Ya on Nanking Road, opened in 1927, one of the best-known Cantonese establishments in the city and a normal place for a well-dressed man to be seen. Zhou Enlai ran the Communist Party's underground apparatus in Shanghai in the late 1920s and early 1930s, when discovery meant death; the point of the story is that concealment worked best in the most public place available.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: you will have served those who come after as a teacher by negative example
fm02_qianyan.note: 反面教员, "negative-example teacher," a term of art in Chinese political language of the period: a person or thing whose bad example instructs. It was applied to former enemies, to purged officials, and eventually to almost anyone. Here it is the precise job description Zhou Enlai is offering, and it is the commission under which this entire book was written. Every page that follows is shaped by it.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: counts as a further confession, and the government will certainly not call you to account for it
fm02_qianyan.note: The assurance is the hinge of the book's reliability, and it cuts both ways. It removes the strongest reason to conceal — but it also creates an incentive to over-confess, since the value of the testimony to those commissioning it rises with how damning it is. Both pressures should be kept in mind at every point where Shen Zui reports his own crimes.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: what is asked of you is truth, not completeness
fm02_qianyan.note: 要求真实，不求全面. Chen Yi's formula is the editorial charter of the whole Selected Historical Materials project, and it is a genuinely good one for memoir evidence: it asks the witness for what he actually knows rather than for a coherent account, and it explicitly forbids filling gaps. What follows immediately — Chen Yi striking out material that magnified his own part — shows the other edge of the same policy.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: so he had struck all of it out
fm02_qianyan.note: Worth pausing on. In the same breath in which he demands truth and forbids invention, Chen Yi describes deleting accounts of his own guerrilla campaigns because they credited him too much and the Party too little. The standard being set is not simply accuracy; it is accuracy within a frame that requires collective rather than individual agency. That frame operates throughout this book too.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: the seventh day of the lunar year
fm02_qianyan.note: 21 February 1961 was indeed the seventh day of the first lunar month, which is a small but real check on the date: the two calendars agree. The seventh day, 人日 or "Humans' Day," is traditionally the birthday of humankind. Nothing in the text makes anything of that, but it is why the countryside was still keeping the festival.

奉谕速办. This is the sharpest documentary observation in the book, and it is the observation of a man who had the files in his hands. 谕 is the word for a superior's directive and, historically, for an imperial edict; 奉谕 says an order has been received without saying from whom. Shen Zui's point is that the Juntong's killing orders were papered in a formula that recorded authority while naming nobody, so that the archive proves an instruction existed and can never show whose it was. It is a claim about deniability by design, made from the inside, and it is checkable in principle against surviving Nationalist files.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: more than a hundred martyrs were cruelly put to death
fm02_qianyan.note: The Chungking massacre of 27 November 1949, at the Zhazidong and Baigongguan prisons on the eve of the city's fall, in which political prisoners were machine-gunned and the buildings burned. The dead are usually numbered in the low hundreds; the prisons were part of the compound the Sino-American Cooperative Organization had used, which is why the massacre and SACO are permanently linked in Chinese memory. Shen Zui devotes a later chapter to that organization.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: "Child, you may go without office, but you must be a decent human being."
fm02_qianyan.note: 你可以不做官，但要做人. The force of the line is in 做人 — literally "to be/act as a person," meaning to conduct oneself as a human being ought — set against 做官, "to be an official." The pairing makes office and decency alternatives rather than companions. The same phrase supplies the title of the 1980 People's Daily interview reprinted at the end of this book, where Shen Zui says he only learned what 做人 meant after 1949; the preface and the closing piece are bound together by it.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: I have left out the names of some of them, clearly as I remember those names
fm02_qianyan.note: An editorial decision worth noticing, because it is the one place in the preface where Shen Zui says outright that he is withholding something he knows. His stated reason is to protect the relatives; the effect is that the book's account of defectors from the Communist Party is deliberately incomplete in exactly the respect readers would most want to check.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: In 1975, when Zheng Xilin came to Peking on a study visit
fm02_qianyan.note: 1975 is when the last group of imprisoned Nationalist personnel was pardoned, and the "study visits" to Peking were part of that programme. So the verification Shen Zui describes — checking the founding roster with two surviving members of the original group — was possible only because both men had outlived the service, the civil war and twenty-five years of captivity or obscurity. It is also the best evidence in the book of his working method: he checked what he could, with the few people alive who could check it.

ch01.anchor: using resistance to Japan as the pretext, he began energetically preparing for work whose muzzles pointed inward
ch01.note: 枪口对内, "muzzles pointed inward" -- turning the guns on one's own people rather than the invader. The phrase was a standing Communist accusation against the Nationalists in these years, and Shen Zui uses it here of his own service without comment. It is the book's characteristic move: the vocabulary of the accusation has become the vocabulary of the confession.

ch01.anchor: After fighting broke out in Shanghai on 13 August
ch01.note: The Battle of Shanghai, which began on 13 August 1937 and ran three months. It was the largest engagement of the war to that point; Chinese losses were enormous, Shanghai fell in November and Nanking in December. The dates in this paragraph are correct and the sequence -- the plan for a Shanghai or Nanking class overtaken by the speed of the collapse -- matches the record.

ch01.anchor: Every one of these key men was a Communist renegade who had studied in the Soviet Union.
ch01.note: Not a rhetorical flourish. Yu Lexing had been a work-study student in France and then in Moscow; several of the others followed the same route through the Chinese Communist Party's Soviet training in the 1920s before changing sides. Their value to Dai Li was precisely their knowledge of the organization they were now to be used against, and the chapter returns to it later, where renegades teach the course on penetrating Communist organizations and find the work "full of contradiction and very painful."

ch01.anchor: this Trotskyite bandit
ch01.note: 托派匪徒. Liang Ganqiao was a Whampoa first-class graduate who had studied in Moscow and been expelled from the Chinese Communist Party in the Trotskyist purge of 1929 before joining Dai Li's service. In the political language of the period "Trotskyite" had become an all-purpose term of abuse largely detached from Trotsky's politics, and by the 1960s, when Shen Zui was writing, it was among the heaviest labels available. He applies it in passing, as a fact rather than a judgement.

ch01.anchor: more than eleven hundred
ch01.note: The class's size is given three ways in this chapter -- more than eleven hundred at the opening, about seven hundred left by graduation, and "about a thousand" as the number of agents it produced -- and the differences are accounted for in the text by early postings, desertions and withdrawals. The figures are internally consistent, which is worth noting in a memoir written from memory twenty-four years later.

ch01.anchor: Hu Zongnan
ch01.note: Hu Zongnan (1896-1962), Whampoa first class, Chiang Kai-shek's most favoured field commander and from 1937 the dominant military figure in the north-west. He appears throughout this book as a rival power centre to the Juntong; a later chapter is devoted to his dealings with Dai Li and Mao Renfeng. His transfer of sixty women cadets here, against their wishes, is characteristic of how the two organizations traded people.

ch01.anchor: the Central Military Academy's Seventh Branch
ch01.note: The Whampoa academy, renamed the Central Military Academy after 1928, ran numbered branch schools during the war. The Seventh Branch, at Xi'an, was Hu Zongnan's. The women recruited for it had volunteered to fight Japan, which is exactly the objection they raise a few pages later on discovering what the Linli class actually was.

ch01.anchor: the Binli Alumni Association
ch01.note: 滨澧同学会, "the association of those from the banks of the Li" -- the Li being the river at Linli. Shen Zui's chairmanship of it, described at length later in this chapter, is one of the clearest passages in the book about how patronage actually worked inside the Juntong: he funded the association out of Juntong property he was liquidating, and traded placements for the goodwill of the men who controlled the service.

ch01.anchor: the Yunong Embankment
ch01.note: 雨农堤. Yunong, "rain farmer," was Dai Li's style-name, the literary alternative name a Chinese man of his generation used alongside his given name. Naming a walk in the grounds after the absent director is the kind of courtship the chapter is full of; it did Yu Lexing no good at all in the end.

ch01.anchor: a director's office was set up all the same, with Ding Ruoping appointed as its secretary, as a check on the deputy director
ch01.note: The structural point of the whole chapter in one sentence. Dai Li never worked at the class, yet maintained an office there whose function was to watch the man who did. The same design recurs at every level of the organization described in this book, and Shen Zui states it without any suggestion that it was unusual.

ch01.anchor: the head of political training, Wang Zuhua
ch01.note: The political training office is the ideological apparatus of the class, and its head is described here in one breath as an anti-Communist propagandist, the man responsible for "pumping in fascist doctrine," and the officer who vetted the students' opinions. The three functions were not distinguished in practice, which is the point.

ch01.anchor: This woman agent was famous for her ferocity, and even her husband, Xu Yuyi, had been on the receiving end of her pistol.
ch01.note: One of a handful of moments where the roster breaks into anecdote. The Juntong recruited women in numbers and used them for work its men could not do -- surveillance in hotels and households, the "working wives" described below -- and the book's women agents are drawn with the same flat matter-of-factness as its men.

ch01.anchor: Fan Xuewen, Jiang Zhennan, Feng Wenyao and Wang Weizhou
ch01.note: Four men "just back from studying secret-service work in Germany and Italy." Nationalist China sent officers to both fascist states through the 1930s, and Germany supplied China's most important military mission until it was withdrawn in 1938 under Japanese pressure. Jiang Zhennan reappears a few pages later as the author of the class song, adapted from a Nazi party anthem. Jiang Zhennan's name was crop-verified: the OCR gave two different wrong readings of it on the same page.

ch01.anchor: Jin Minjie, a Korean
ch01.note: Koreans in Chinese service were common in this period: after Japan's annexation of Korea in 1910 a large exile community formed in China, and the Korean independence movement worked closely with both Nationalists and Communists. Jin Minjie teaches unarmed combat here, kills a student in a training bout later in the chapter, and is promoted to deputy director of the Juntong's combat class.

ch01.anchor: whichever one they fancied as a "working wife."
ch01.note: 工作太太. The term is the organization's own, and the arrangement it names -- a woman assigned to an agent going into occupied territory, to make his cover plausible and to serve as his household -- was routine. Shen Zui reports it in the same register as the issue of clothing allowances. Nothing in the text suggests the women were consulted.

ch01.anchor: the party anthem of the German fascists
ch01.note: The Horst-Wessel-Lied, the Nazi Party's anthem and from 1933 effectively a second German national anthem. That the Juntong's own song began as an adaptation of it, produced by an instructor fresh from training in Germany, is Shen Zui's joke and also his evidence. The claim is uncorroborated outside this account and is difficult to test, since the surviving Chinese words are not a translation of the German.

ch01.anchor: "safeguard the security of our leader, defend the territory and sovereignty of the state"
ch01.note: 维护我们领袖的安全，保卫国家领土和主权. Shen Zui's point is the order of the two clauses, and Dai Li's pleasure in them. In a song adopted in the second year of a war of national survival, the leader's personal safety comes first and the country's territory second. That is the argument of the passage, and it is made simply by quoting.

ch01.anchor: *Appendix: the words of the class song.
ch01.note: TRANSLATOR'S NOTE. The book prints the full lyric at this point. It is characterised here rather than set out line by line; the two lines that carry Shen Zui's argument are quoted in the paragraph above, where he makes it. Nothing in the argument depends on the remaining text, which is conventional period exhortation. The Chinese is on printed page 20 of the third edition for anyone who wants it.

ch01.anchor: they had thrown down the pen and taken up arms in order to fight Japan, and they had no wish to be secret agents
ch01.note: 投笔从戎, "to throw down the writing-brush and join the army," from the biography of the Han general Ban Chao, who abandoned a copyist's desk for the frontier. The phrase carries real weight in this sentence: these were students who had volunteered out of patriotism and found themselves conscripted into political police work. Of the whole chapter this is the one moment where the people being trained get to state their own position.

ch01.anchor: swearing collectively to join the Juntong
ch01.note: The device is the chapter's most quietly chilling passage, and Shen Zui explains the reasoning himself two paragraphs later: get the formalities of membership done before the students learn what the work is, and "with the chain already round their necks, they could be dealt with." It became standard practice at every subsequent Juntong class.

ch01.anchor: the great victory at Pingxingguan
ch01.note: The engagement of 25 September 1937 in north-eastern Shanxi, in which the Communist Eighth Route Army's 115th Division ambushed a Japanese supply column and destroyed it. Militarily it was a small action; politically it was enormous, the first clear Chinese victory of the war and proof that the Communists were fighting. That is precisely why the class's political officer had to explain it away, and why the students' response -- so even a battle the Communist army wins is a fake -- was so hard to answer.

ch01.anchor: the *New China Daily*
ch01.note: 新华日报, the Chinese Communist Party's newspaper, published legally in Nationalist territory from Hankow in 1938 and then in Chungking until 1947 under the terms of the United Front. Its legality is what makes this passage possible: the students were reading a paper the government permitted, and the class treated possession of it as grounds for secret surveillance.

ch01.anchor: the Lu Xun Academy of Arts in Yenan
ch01.note: 鲁迅艺术学院, founded in Yenan (modern pinyin Yan'an) in April 1938, the Communist base area's school for writers, artists and musicians. That students at Linli had friends and classmates there, writing to urge them to get out, places the two institutions in the same generation of Chinese young people, sorted by little more than which recruiter reached them first.

ch01.anchor: the agents built a detention room at the class headquarters
ch01.note: TRANSLATION NOTE: 禁闭室, a military detention cell rather than a prison. The OCR read the second character as 财 throughout this passage, which is meaningless here; the reading is from context and is not in doubt.

ch01.anchor: the excellence of the application lies in the mind of the one who applies it
ch01.note: 运用之妙，存乎一心, from the biography of Yue Fei in the History of the Song, where the general answers a question about battle formations by saying that the formation is only the beginning and everything depends on the commander's judgement. It is one of the most famous lines in Chinese military writing. Shen Zui's gloss on what it was taken to mean in the Juntong -- stick at nothing, take no account of any law -- is his own, and the deflation is deliberate.

ch01.anchor: a demolition instructor named Cai
ch01.note: The book gives only the surname. Where a name is incomplete or redacted in the source it is left so here rather than filled in; the redactions later in this chapter, printed as XX in the Chinese, are the author's own or his editors'.

ch01.anchor: Bringing a man down from the third or fourth floor, for example, raises the nice question of whether the operations agent should go in front or behind
ch01.note: This paragraph and the two that follow are the closest thing in the book to a technical manual, and they are the reason it was written. The Juntong's arrest methods were taught orally and never printed -- Shen Zui says so explicitly below -- so a participant's recollection is close to the only source there is. Read as evidence, the passage is unusually credible: it is specific, it is unflattering to the author, and it contains the sort of practical detail nobody inventing an account would think to supply.

ch01.anchor: the cat weeping for the mouse
ch01.note: 猫哭老鼠, the exact Chinese equivalent of crocodile tears -- the cat mourns the mouse it has eaten. Shen Zui applies it to the memorial meeting held for a student the instructors had beaten to death, and the reader should notice that the author was one of the two instructors who beat him.

ch01.anchor: I gave him a heavy blow of the same kind. After these two occasions Yan Xie was so badly injured that he could not be saved
ch01.note: The most direct admission of personal killing in this chapter, made in a single sentence and not returned to. Under the terms of the commission described in the preface, admissions of this kind were what the book existed to produce; that does not make this one less likely to be true, and its very flatness is characteristic. The student's name was crop-verified: the OCR read it two different ways, neither correct.

ch01.anchor: A few drops of croton oil on a piece of beef
ch01.note: 巴豆油, pressed from the seed of Croton tiglium, a violent purgative used in Chinese medicine in minute doses. The book's claim that it kills a dog within half an hour but does a man little harm reflects what was taught at the class rather than pharmacology; croton oil is dangerous to humans in quantity.

ch01.anchor: he was hauled in to serve as "practice material."
ch01.note: 实习品, literally "practice article" -- the word for a specimen or a training aid, applied to a man. The whole episode, in which a doctor suspected of petty embezzlement is publicly tortured through every method the curriculum taught and released without evidence, is offered by Shen Zui as an explanation of what the students learned from it: that the organization stood outside the law entirely.

ch01.anchor: Ye Jianying
ch01.note: Ye Jianying (1897-1986), then Communist chief of staff in the Nationalist-Communist United Front and later one of the People's Republic's marshals. He did teach guerrilla warfare at the Nanyue guerrilla cadre training class in Hunan in early 1939, a genuinely joint Nationalist-Communist institution. Dai Li's response -- planting two of his officers on the course to steal the method for use against its teachers -- is the United Front in miniature.

ch01.anchor: theft is not in itself a capital offence, but as he had failed in his task and shamed Dai Li into the bargain, Dai Li in a rage had him brought back and shot
ch01.note: A summary execution of one of his own battalion commanders, reported in a subordinate clause. The passage is one of several in the book where the scale of Dai Li's personal authority is conveyed not by assertion but by what the narrative treats as unremarkable.

ch01.anchor: a sentry every three paces and a picket every five
ch01.note: 三步一岗，五步一哨, a set phrase for a place under heavy guard. The reception it describes went badly wrong: Dai Li read the display as a warlord's, and his objection -- that if Chiang Kai-shek heard of him putting on airs like this, where would it end -- says a good deal about how precarious the position of even the most feared man in the service was.

ch01.anchor: a Henanese woman student, Liu Ying, who had never been in the water in her life, was drowned
ch01.note: Two deaths are recorded at this class, both in training: this drowning and the beating of Yan Xie. Both surface only because a political instructor used them as ammunition against his superiors at a staff meeting, which is a fair indication of how such things were normally handled.

ch01.anchor: Tang Shengming, then garrison commander there, together with his wife Xu Lai
ch01.note: Tang Shengming (1906-1987) was the younger brother of the general Tang Shengzhi and later went over to the Japanese-sponsored Nanking government at Dai Li's direction, as a planted agent -- one of the more remarkable arrangements of the war. Xu Lai (1909-1973) was among the best-known film actresses of 1930s Shanghai before her marriage. Their appearance here as weekend guests at a graduation ceremony is a fair sample of the world the Juntong moved in.

ch01.anchor: they wept as though for their own parents
ch01.note: 如丧考妣, "as though mourning father and mother," a set phrase that is almost always sardonic in modern usage. Shen Zui is describing his own students, and himself among their patrons, at the moment their protector died.

ch01.anchor: nothing that was not Li was proper and nothing that was not Li would be used
ch01.note: 非澧不视，非澧不用 -- a pun that cannot survive into English. 澧, the Li of Linli, is a homophone of 礼, ritual propriety, and the phrase parodies a famous passage of the Analects in which Confucius tells Yan Hui to look at nothing improper and do nothing improper. The old agents' complaint is thus that promotion now depends not on propriety but on having been at Linli. The English keeps the shape and loses the joke, which is why it is glossed here.

ch01.anchor: instead of "comrade" they said "fellow student,"
ch01.note: 同学 against 同志. "Comrade" was the Juntong's own internal form of address, borrowed like much of its vocabulary from the movement it existed to destroy; the Linli graduates' preference for "fellow student" was a way of marking a narrower and more useful loyalty. The distinction runs through the rest of the chapter.

ch01.anchor: the great destruction and the massacre at Chungking
ch01.note: The demolitions and prison killings carried out in Chungking in late November 1949 as the Nationalists abandoned the city. Political prisoners at the Zhazidong and Baigongguan gaols were shot and the buildings fired; the dead numbered in the low hundreds. The Bath Cave named here, 渣滓洞, is Zhazidong itself -- a former coal pit whose name means "dross pit." These prisons stood in the compound the Sino-American Cooperative Organization had used, which is why the two are inseparable in Chinese memory; a later chapter of this book is devoted to that organization.

ch01.anchor: His own wife, whose name I withhold, was an underground Party member he had arrested; he raped her, took her by force as his wife, and made her publish a notice in the press renouncing the Party.
ch01.note: The book prints the man's surname followed by XX, redacting the rest, and gives the woman no name at all. Both redactions are the source's and are preserved. Published renunciations of Communist Party membership were a standard instrument of the Nationalist security services, extracted under duress and printed in the newspapers as evidence of the Party's collapse.

ch01.anchor: Mao Sen
ch01.note: Mao Sen (1908-1964), Juntong officer, head of the Shanghai garrison inspectorate and then of police and security in Shanghai before its fall in 1949; he directed the executions of political prisoners in the city's last months and went on to Taiwan, where he was shot dead in Japan in 1964 in circumstances never established. He is among the most notorious figures in this book's cast and is named here without elaboration.

ch01.anchor: After Hu Zongnan attacked Yenan in 1947
ch01.note: Hu Zongnan's forces took Yenan (modern pinyin Yan'an) on 19 March 1947, after the Communist leadership had already evacuated it. The city was held for just over a year and recovered in April 1948. That the Juntong immediately installed an investigation office there, headed by a Linli graduate, is the detail Shen Zui wants: the occupation of an emptied town was still worth a secret-service establishment.

ch01.anchor: the Juntong selected to study in the United States just after the war against Japan ended
ch01.note: American training of Nationalist intelligence personnel followed directly from the wartime Sino-American Cooperative Organization, which had put US Navy instructors into Chinese secret-service training classes from 1943. The resentment Shen Zui records -- that two junior graduates were sent alongside departmental heads -- is a small measure of how valuable the American connection was thought to be.

ch01.anchor: are carrying on their evil work in Taiwan to this day
ch01.note: "To this day" means the early 1960s, when this chapter was written, not the 1995 or 2001 of publication. The book was composed in a period when the Nationalist government on Taiwan was an active adversary and its intelligence services were running operations against the mainland; the present tense here is a live one, and it is the tense in which the whole book's closing judgements are made.

ch03.anchor: saving the nation by a curved path
ch03.note: 曲线救国, literally 'saving the nation by a curved path': the argument that a Nationalist commander might defect to the Japanese-backed regime and preserve his forces to fight the Communists, thereby serving China indirectly. It was used to excuse large-scale defections after 1941. Shen Zui states flatly that the Juntong executed this policy. The charge is standard in post-1949 mainland writing; the scale of Nationalist defection is documented, though the extent to which it was centrally directed rather than opportunistic remains disputed in scholarship.

陪都, the 'accompanying capital'. Chungking held this status from 1937, Nanking remaining the nominal capital. The term implies a subordinate seat holding the government in trust rather than a replacement for it.

Zhang Jianzhai (1880-1950), among the best-known practitioners of Chinese medicine of his generation, from Nanking, who moved to Chungking during the war and treated senior Nationalist figures. Shen Zui's account of operatives loitering about his consulting room, and of a companion attending him while he smoked opium in order to draw him out, is uncorroborated and rests on the author's own testimony.

Guo Jiqiao (1902-1971), a career officer close to Hu Zongnan, later chief of the general staff on Taiwan. The episode that follows, in which he is rebuffed by the Inspectorate and told the Generalissimo's approval places it beyond his reach, is Shen Zui's illustration of a point he makes repeatedly: the Juntong's overt bodies wore the uniform of the commands that nominally housed them and answered to none of them.

袍哥, the 'gowned brothers', the dominant secret-society network of Szechwan, comparable in function to the Green Gang in Shanghai. Membership ran through commerce, local administration and the professions, which is why the Juntong found a Paoko steward worth recruiting.

Liu Zhi (1892-1971), one of Chiang Kai-shek's senior commanders, remembered for a series of defeats; Wang Zanxu (1885-1960), a Szechwanese warlord who held provincial and garrison office and remained on the mainland after 1949. The book prints his surname-name as 王瓒绪; scholarship generally gives 王缵绪. Preserved as printed.

ch03.anchor: Inspectorate of the Chungking Garrison Command
ch03.note: The book prints 卫成总司令部 throughout, twelve times, where the institution is unmistakably the 重庆卫戍总司令部, the Chungking Garrison Command. 卫成 is not a word. Every occurrence reads 成 in the scan rather than 戍, and the two characters differ by a single stroke. A printing error and a substitution introduced by the JBIG2 compression of this scan are both possible and cannot be told apart at this resolution. Translated by the institution actually meant.

Chen Duxiu (1879-1942), a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and its first general secretary, expelled in 1929 after aligning with the Left Opposition, imprisoned by the Nationalists 1932-1937 and living out his last years at Jiangjin upriver from Chungking. The surveillance Shen Zui describes is consistent with the known outline of those years. His report of Chen's conversation -- that the Communist Party should operate under Nationalist leadership, and praise of Chiang Kai-shek as indispensable -- should be read with care: it is a Juntong officer's recollection, written decades later under conditions where Chen's reputation was fixed, and it is exactly the account most useful to the teller.

Zhang Guotao (1897-1979), a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and Mao's chief rival in the mid-1930s, who defected to the Nationalists in 1938 and ran a research and training operation for the Juntong. His appearance here as a Kiangsi provincial councillor making connections for the Juntong, and earlier as the trainer of its anti-Communist specialists, is corroborated in outline by other accounts of his post-defection career.

Song Meiling (1898-2003), Chiang Kai-shek's wife, held this post from 1936 and was closely involved in aircraft procurement and in the recruitment of the American Volunteer Group. Allegations of corruption in aviation purchasing circulated widely at the time. The anonymous letter Shen Zui describes, and the fifteen-year sentence that followed, are not independently documented; the episode is his own.

Kong Lingjun (1919-1994), second daughter of H. H. Kung and Song Ailing, known universally as 孔二小姐, Miss Kung the Second. Her habit of dressing in men's clothes and her reputation for arrogance were widely remarked in wartime Chungking, and she became a standing symbol of the privileges of the ruling families.

Song Xilian (1907-1993), a Whampoa graduate and Nationalist lieutenant-general, captured in 1949 and pardoned in 1959 -- the same programme of pardons that released Shen Zui, and the same 文史资料 system that produced this book collected his memoirs too.

锦衣卫, the Jinyiwei, the Ming dynasty's imperial secret police, who held powers of arrest, interrogation and execution outside the ordinary judicial system and whose name became a byword for terror. That Juntong operatives applied it to their own action group, behind its back, is one of the sharpest things in the chapter: the men doing the work reached for the oldest available word for what they were.

The Juntong's own graded nickname for its prisons: the corps detention house at Wanglongmen the 'Elementary School', Baigongguan the 'Middle School', and the Xifeng concentration camp the 'University', a prisoner ascending as his case grew more serious. Baigongguan and Zhazidong, both inside the SACO compound, became after 1949 the best-known sites of Nationalist political imprisonment in China and are now museums.

ch03.anchor: Is Mr. Wang Sixin at home?
ch03.note: Untranslatable as it stands. The traditional form of 宪 (xian), for 宪兵, the military police, is 憲, which decomposes into the elements 王, 四 and 心 -- wang, si, xin. A waiter calling out for 'Mr. Wang Sixin' was spelling out the character for the military police in the hearing of guests who needed warning. The English keeps the name and explains the device; there is no way to carry the puzzle itself across.

Liao Chengzhi (1908-1983), son of the Nationalist leader Liao Zhongkai, a senior Communist held by the Nationalists from 1942 until 1946, and after 1949 a central figure in overseas Chinese affairs. His detention alongside Ye Ting is documented.

Ye Ting (1896-1946), commander of the New Fourth Army, captured in January 1941 when Nationalist forces destroyed his headquarters in the New Fourth Army Incident, and held until 1946. He died in an air crash weeks after his release. The sequence of his confinement given here -- Wanglongmen, then Baigongguan, then the Honglu factory, with an interval at Enshi where Chen Cheng tried to talk him into surrender -- matches the general record. Shen Zui devotes a later chapter to him.

Tang Shaoyi (1862-1938), the first premier of the Republic, assassinated at his Shanghai home in September 1938. Nationalist agents were widely held responsible, on the suspicion that he was preparing to join a Japanese-sponsored government. Shen Zui's detail here -- that the Juntong used a relative to reach him -- is consistent with accounts that the killers gained entry as antique dealers, though he does not name the man he calls Xie Zhipan's connection.

The Sino-American Cooperative Organization (中美合作所), established 1943 under Dai Li and the American naval officer Milton Miles, providing training, weapons and communications equipment to the Juntong. Its compound at Geleshan outside Chungking held the Baigongguan and Zhazidong prisons. Shen Zui writes of it throughout in the idiom required of him -- 美帝, 'the American imperialists' -- and devotes a later chapter to it.

Milton E. Miles (1900-1961), United States Navy officer, head of the American side of SACO and Dai Li's principal foreign partner. American accounts present SACO as a wartime intelligence and weather-reporting arrangement; mainland accounts, this one included, present it as equipping the Juntong's domestic repression. Both are describing the same organization.

红岩村 at Hualongqiao, seat of the Communist Party's South China Bureau and of its delegation in Chungking through the war. It is now a museum. Shen Zui's account of the surveillance mounted against it -- a two-tier arrangement, an inspection picket, and an attempt to place a line inside the *Xinhua Daily* that failed -- is the fullest description of the operation from the watching side.

曾家岩 50, the Chungking office of the Communist delegation, known as the Zhou Residence, where Zhou Enlai lived and received visitors. Also now a museum. The rule Shen Zui reports -- that a guest seen out by Zhou Enlai in person need not be followed, but a man who let himself in and pulled the door shut behind him must be -- is a working detail of the kind that rarely survives into the record.

Shi Liang (1900-1985), lawyer, the only woman among the 'Seven Gentlemen' arrested in 1936 for agitating for resistance to Japan, and after 1949 the People's Republic's first Minister of Justice. Shen Junru, named alongside her, was another of the Seven. Song Qingling, the widow of Sun Yat-sen, was the most prominent figure the Nationalists could not touch directly.

ch03.anchor: Guo Moruo, Tian Han, Cao Yu
ch03.note: Three of the leading literary figures of wartime Chungking: Guo Moruo (1892-1978), poet, historian and head of the cultural work committee; Tian Han (1898-1968), dramatist and author of the words of the national anthem; Cao Yu (1910-1996), the foremost playwright of the period. That a small beef house served as the observation post for all three is the chapter's characteristic register: the apparatus is vast and its methods are shabby.

John Leighton Stuart (1876-1962), missionary educator, president of Yenching University and from 1946 United States ambassador to China. The detail that the arrested woman teacher was the sister of one of his secretaries places her in the missionary-educational world rather than the Party, which makes what follows worse rather than better.

Du Yuesheng (1888-1951), head of the Green Gang and the dominant figure of the Shanghai underworld, who moved to Chungking during the war. His relations with Dai Li were close and long-standing. Shen Zui treats his usefulness -- secret-society work, introductions, information -- as unremarkable.

Dai Chuanxian, better known as Dai Jitao (1891-1949), a founding theorist of Nationalist ideology and president of the Examination Yuan for twenty years. The anecdote that follows, in which his own aide invented the theft of a vase, is told against the servants of the great houses rather than against Dai Jitao.

Yu Dawei (1897-1993), director of the Ordnance Administration through the war and later defence minister on Taiwan, a Harvard-trained mathematician regarded as one of the most capable technocrats in the Nationalist government. Shen Zui's account of the bargain struck with him -- the Juntong gets the workers, Yu keeps the accounts -- and of Dai Li having an informant shot to placate him, is uncorroborated and among the more serious allegations in the chapter.

Lin Kesheng, known in English as Robert Lim (1897-1969), physiologist, founder of the Chinese Red Cross Medical Relief Corps and director of the Army Medical Administration, one of the most distinguished scientists in wartime China. He appears here in a list of men Dai Li 'made direct use of', a characterization Shen Zui offers without evidence and which should be weighed against Lim's record.

Bei Zuyi (1893-1982), banker, at various times head of the Bank of China's foreign exchange operations and later governor of the Central Bank. His family later became known in the West through his nephew, the architect I. M. Pei.

Wang Pengsheng (1893-1946), head of the International Affairs Research Institute, a Japan specialist whose organization produced strategic intelligence for the Nationalist government and operated in some tension with the Juntong.

He Chengjun (1882-1961), a senior Nationalist general of the older generation. Zeng Yangfu (1898-1969), named with him, was an engineer and administrator responsible for wartime transport. The passage is Shen Zui's clearest statement of Dai Li's method: draft an establishment on someone else's paper, take the real power and the machinery, and stay junior in appearance.

The Lin Shiliang case, 1942: an official of the Central Trust connected to H. H. Kung, tried and executed for smuggling. It was among the most publicized corruption prosecutions of the war and was widely read as a demonstration that the Nationalist government would act against the powerful. Shen Zui's reading is the opposite and is worth the note: the man died, in his account, not because the law reached him but because he failed to approach Dai Li in time and then forced a matter into the open that Dai Li could not be seen to drop.

Ren Yuandao (1890-1980) and Zhou Fohai (1897-1948) were senior figures in Wang Jingwei's Japanese-sponsored government at Nanking; Zhou was among its most important, and was convicted of treason after the war. Shen Zui's claim that their representatives were received at Juntong headquarters, escorted by the head of the Chungking Inspectorate, is the hinge of his argument that Chungking had no traitor problem it wished to solve. Contact between Chungking and Nanking through intermediaries is documented; the particular scene is his.

ch03.anchor: aiding the tyrant in his cruelty
ch03.note: 助桀为虐, to help Jie in his tyranny -- Jie being the last ruler of the Xia, a byword for cruelty. The commoner form of the idiom substitutes Zhou, the last Shang ruler (助纣为虐). The book prints Jie; preserved as printed.

清水衙门, a 'clear-water yamen': an office with no opportunities for graft, the water being clear because there is no fat in it. The complementary phrase in the same passage, that the censors were 'picking bones out of waste paper', is the staff's own.

国民参政会, an advisory body convened from 1938 which gave the Communists, the minor parties and independents a public platform without giving them power. Its sessions were the moments at which non-Nationalist opinion could be heard in Chungking, which is why, as Shen Zui explains, they were the Juntong's busiest weeks.

中央训练团, through which Nationalist civil and military cadres were rotated for political indoctrination. Shen Zui's point is that the guard group placed inside it reported what trainees said, and that those reports entered Chiang Kai-shek's personnel assessments -- so that the course was also a screening.

抗日锄奸团, organized in the north Chinese universities after 1931 to act against collaborators. Shen Zui records Dai Li's own redefinition of its purpose after the move to Szechwan: the 奸 to be 'hoed out' had been the traitor to China and was now the traitor within, meaning Communists. The English cannot keep the single character doing both jobs.
The clash of 7 July 1937 south of Peiping which began the full Sino-Japanese war.
The Japanese seizure of Manchuria beginning 18 September 1931, the event that produced the student patriotic organizations from which the Anti-Traitor Corps grew.

Chen Lifu (1900-2001) and his brother Chen Guofu led the CC Clique, which controlled the Nationalist party apparatus and its own intelligence service, the Zhongtong. The Juntong and the Zhongtong were rivals throughout, and the deference Dai Li shows here over a single opened letter measures the Chens' standing.

中统, the Central Statistics Bureau, the Nationalist party's intelligence organization, run through the CC Clique and the Juntong's standing rival. Where this book says 'the Juntong' it means the military service; the two organizations competed for cases, budgets and Chiang Kai-shek's attention.

十人团, an inner group of Dai Li's earliest and most trusted subordinates, repeatedly used to name the men placed at the head of newly captured organizations. Shen Zui names its members across several chapters.

The Whampoa Military Academy, founded 1924 near Canton with Chiang Kai-shek as commandant. A man's Whampoa intake number functioned throughout the Nationalist army as a marker of seniority and of who his patrons were, which is why Shen Zui records it so often.

美帝. The term is not the translator's. It is the standard designation in mainland Chinese writing of the 1950s and 1960s and its use here is a condition of the book's publication, applied even to equipment Shen Zui was requesting and receiving at the time. The register is preserved throughout rather than neutralized; where the author's contemporary self and his writing self are at odds, the seam is the evidence.

Gu Zhenggang (1902-1974), Minister of Social Affairs, later on Taiwan. The anecdote of the doctored price board is offered by Shen Zui as propaganda he did not believe, and he closes it by pointing out that the Juntong reported real prices to Chiang Kai-shek daily.

渣滓洞, a former coal pit inside the SACO compound converted into a prison, and with Baigongguan the best known site of Nationalist political imprisonment. Most of those held there were killed in the days before the Communist entry into Chungking in November 1949.

Zhu Zongliang led the Anti-Traitor Corps south after 1937. Shen Zui's account of Dai Li receiving the corps' students in Chengtu in batches over successive evenings, dining and dancing with them, is characteristic of the personal management by which Dai Li held the organization together.

Yu Zuobai (1889-1959), a Kwangsi military figure who briefly held the provincial governorship in 1929 before breaking with Chiang Kai-shek. His value to the Juntong, as Shen Zui presents it, lay precisely in his connections among Chiang's opponents.
The book prints 王固盘; the form found in scholarship is 王固磐 (1900-1965), commissioner of the Nanking capital police. Preserved as printed.
三斗坪, on the Yangtze in western Hupeh, close to the front line after the fall of Ichang in 1940 and a crossing point between occupied and unoccupied China.

息烽, in Kweichow, site of the Juntong's largest concentration camp, where prisoners judged most serious were held. Its position at the top of the 'Elementary School, Middle School, University' scale is the author's own usage.

The passage renders the cant of the Chungking thieves as the detectives repeated it: 吃洋火钱 for picking pockets, 拣露水钱 for the dawn housebreaker working door to door, 吃灯花 for the thief who waits until the lamps are lit. The images survive translation; the point Shen Zui is making does not depend on them, which is that his men could sort a professional at sight and arrested novices instead.

The Chinese counts characters where English counts words: 望龙门 is three characters, and 望龙门的, 'of Wanglongmen', is four. The counts are kept because the passage turns on the name being short enough to be flung at people as a threat.

军统局重庆特区, abbreviated 渝特区, the Juntong's field organization for Chungking and eastern Szechwan, distinct from the bureau headquarters in the same city. Shen Zui's judgement of it is unusually direct: it could show no results against the Communists because its men had no standing in society and could reach no further than the middling ranks of the minor parties.

纪念周, the weekly assembly at which Nationalist organizations gathered for political instruction, nominally in memory of Sun Yat-sen. Dai Li used the Juntong's for exhortation and for the public warnings Shen Zui quotes.

Zhou Enlai (1898-1976) headed the Communist delegation in Chungking through the war. Two passages here bear on him: the destruction of letters addressed to him at the postal censorship post, and his declining to demand the life of the squad leader whose shot killed one of his staff. Shen Zui reports both without comment.

Mao Zedong came to Chungking in August 1945 for six weeks of negotiations with Chiang Kai-shek. Shen Zui's account of Dai Li ordering covert protection for him -- and disarming an operative who suggested killing him -- is offered as evidence of calculation rather than restraint: the reckoning, in Dai Li's phrase as Shen Zui gives it, would have fallen on the Juntong.

Song Ziwen (1891-1971), banker and foreign minister, brother of Song Meiling and Song Qingling, and one of the 'Four Great Families' whose protection the chapter describes. The Chinese calls him 国舅, the brother-in-law of the ruling house, a term from imperial usage that the English renders literally.

新华日报, the Communist Party's newspaper, published openly in Chungking from 1938 under the terms of the united front. The chapter's running comedy -- newsboys beaten, papers seized at the road junctions, and the paper on Dai Li's desk the next morning all the same -- is Shen Zui's, and so is the observation that the Inspectorate paid for its subscription.

跑二排, literally 'running the second row': the unpaid or casually paid auxiliaries a field operative recruited and ran himself. Shen Zui counts them separately from the establishment and puts them at more than twenty thousand in Chungking alone, which is how a service of a few thousand covered a city.

外围分子, those worked by the Juntong without being enrolled in it. The distinction matters throughout: Dai Li deliberately kept most of his contacts outside the organization, and of nearly a thousand contacts run by the detective brigade, only about a dozen were Juntong members.

ch03.anchor: one bed built on top of another
ch03.note: 架床叠屋, beds stacked on beds and rooms on rooms: pointless duplication. Shen Zui applies it to the proliferation of overlapping inspection bodies, and the chapter then spends several pages demonstrating it.
瘟神, the gods of pestilence, whose images were floated away on rafts to be rid of them. Used of a person who brings disaster and cannot be shaken off.
鬼门关, the pass into the underworld. What drivers and travellers called the Yipinchang checkpoint behind its commander's back.
勾勾搭搭, an idiom of furtive collusion with a suggestion of the illicit about it. The English keeps the sense and loses the faint disreputability.
贼眉贼眼, 'thief's brows and thief's eyes'. The scan reads 眉 where the commoner form of the idiom has 头. Preserved as printed.

皇后饭店 at Huixianqiao, among the largest Chinese and Western restaurants in wartime Chungking. The list that follows -- restaurants, a dance hall, auction houses, a photographic studio, hotels -- is Shen Zui's inventory of the commercial cover the Juntong ran in the city, and it is the fullest such list in the book.

The studio's purpose, as Shen Zui gives it, was to photograph air passengers and later to undercut its competitors on identity-card work so that the files gained more faces. A clear instance of what the chapter documents: commercial fronts run at a loss for the intelligence they produced.

ch03.anchor: until you could not sleep in peace
ch03.note: The passage around this is written in the second person -- 你 throughout -- addressing the reader as the person searched, tailed and listened to. The English keeps the 'you'. It is the one sustained stylistic departure in an otherwise flatly documentary chapter, and it comes exactly where Shen Zui is describing what his own service did to ordinary people.

Shen Zui's account of putting up a box at the gate for the public to denounce his own men, and opening it himself daily, is characteristic of the book's self-presentation: the reforming officer inside the machine. It sits a few pages from his account of taking part in the design of instruments of torture.

ch03.anchor: I was then, like them, a man who had lost his humanity
ch03.note: One of a handful of places where the confession-and-reform framing required for publication surfaces as a direct first-person judgement rather than as vocabulary. What surrounds it is not softened: he describes contributing to the 'invention' of new instruments and to testing their effects almost daily.

The detention-house hierarchy described here -- a senior inmate of more than two years' standing running the cell, taking half of everything sent in, and keeping order for the warders -- is a recognizable feature of prisons without legal limits on detention. Shen Zui's discovery of it, and his clearing of forty-odd cases in a night, is again the reforming-officer register.
替死鬼, literally a 'substitute-death ghost': the one who dies in another's place. The word recurs through the chapter for those arrested to make up numbers.

ch03.anchor: a thief who steals goes to prison
ch03.note: The saying Shen Zui reports circulating in Chungking is the chapter's theme put in the mouth of the public: the detective brigade built its offices with money taken from thieves and was commended for it.
老板, 'the boss', was how Juntong operatives referred to Dai Li among themselves. The word is deliberately commercial and is kept.

家法, the disciplinary code of a household or clan, applied to its own members outside the state's law. Dai Li's use of the term for the Juntong's internal punishments is exact and revealing: the organization is figured as a family, and its members as subject to a father's discipline rather than a court's.

管家的, the household steward who procures and manages. Dai Li's compliment, as Shen Zui reports it -- and the passage immediately shows its limits, since the same scrounging drew a furious rebuke the moment T. V. Soong's interest lay behind the goods.

设计委员, nominally advisers to the Juntong bureau, in practice a way of retaining people of standing on a stipend against future use. Shen Zui's figure -- that of several hundred, nearly half took the money and did nothing -- and Dai Li's reasoning for keeping them anyway, are among the more candid passages about how the organization spent its funds.
望龙门 on Linsen Road, quarters of the operatives' corps in the Hunan-Hupeh guild hall. The name became a metonym in Chungking for the corps and its violence.

ch04.note: Yang Xingfo was shot in Shanghai on 18 June 1933 and Shi Liangcai on the Shanghai-Hangchow road near Haining on 13 November 1934. Both killings are well documented and both were widely attributed at the time to Nationalist agents. What this chapter adds is the account from inside the organization that carried them out, given by a man who says he collected the material from the officer who directed them.

复兴社, the Renaissance Society, generally known as the Blue Shirts, founded 1932 as a secret Nationalist body on a fascist model. Its Special Services Department was the direct ancestor of the Juntong, which is why Shen Zui has to explain his own 1932 posting through a name the reader will not otherwise recognize.

行动技术, the Juntong's curriculum term covering arrest, assassination, kidnapping and sabotage. Shen Zui states that he edited the lecture notes on it for all the Juntong's special classes and that these two killings were set down in them as teaching material. That is the chapter's warrant: he is not reporting rumour but the case studies he himself taught from.

中国民权保障同盟, founded at the end of 1932 by Song Qingling, Cai Yuanpei and Yang Xingfo to press for the release of political prisoners and for legal protections. It effectively ceased after Yang's assassination. That the League's work was what made Yang a target is the standard account and matches Shen Zui's.

中央研究院, the national academy founded in 1928, of which Yang Xingfo was secretary-general. Its Shanghai premises on Avenue du Roi Albert, where he lived and was shot, are the scene of the first half of this chapter.

Song Qingling (1893-1981), widow of Sun Yat-sen and chairman of the China League for Civil Rights, the most prominent figure in China the Nationalists could not move against directly. Shen Zui's account of the reasoning -- that killing a 'suitable' person near her home was chosen precisely because she could not be touched -- is his own and is consistent with the League's fate.

Now Shaanxi South Road. The insistence on killing Yang inside the French Concession rather than on the open road, which Shen Zui attributes to Chiang Kai-shek directly, turns on the concessions' separate jurisdiction: a killing there embarrassed the foreign police rather than the Chinese government, and demonstrated reach into ground the Nationalists did not control.

Zhao Lijun (1905-1942), head of the East China district's operations group and the Juntong's most used assassin in Shanghai. He was himself executed by the Nationalist government in 1942 after killing a county magistrate in Honan -- a fact Shen Zui records elsewhere in the book. He is named here as Shen Zui's source for both cases.

The killer shot by his own side during the escape, taken alive by the French concession police and, in Shen Zui's account, poisoned in hospital the same evening by a Juntong man serving as a Chinese detective inspector in that force. The newspapers of the day carried only the alias Gao Dechen. That the wounded gunman died in custody is on the record; that he was poisoned to silence him rests on Shen Zui's testimony.

Shen Zui's flattest instance of the Juntong's internal morality: the man Dai Li had killed to protect the operation was afterwards held up to trainees as a hero who took his own life rather than talk, his family compensated, his son raised at the organization's expense, and a road inside the SACO compound named for him. Shen Zui sets the fabrication and the honours side by side without comment.
Yang Xiaofo, Yang Xingfo's son, who was in the car and was wounded in the leg. That the father shielded the boy with his body is the detail by which the killing was remembered.

ch04.anchor: Lu Xun, He Xiangning, Shen Junru and Li Siguang
ch04.note: The mourners the agents watched. Lu Xun (1881-1936), the foremost modern Chinese writer, attended the funeral in defiance of a warning and wrote a well-known quatrain on it. He Xiangning (1878-1972) was a Nationalist elder and painter; Shen Junru (1875-1963) a jurist, later one of the Seven Gentlemen; Li Siguang (1889-1971) the geologist. Shen Zui's point is that the funeral was itself an intelligence operation, everything said there gathered and sent to Nanking.
万国殡仪馆 on Jiaozhou Road, the foreign-run funeral establishment where Yang Xingfo lay and where the memorial was held.
申报, founded 1872 and the most influential Chinese newspaper of its era. Shi Liangcai bought control in 1912 and turned it, by the early 1930s, into a persistent critic of Nationalist rule.

Shi Liangcai (1880-1934), proprietor of the *Shen Bao*. Shen Zui gives the real motive as his sympathy for and financial help to the Communists, and then says something more damaging about himself: that while teaching the case at Chungking he knowingly told students a different reason -- a Japanese-backed Shanghai independence movement, 'the crime of betraying the country' -- because he dared not let them hear the true one. It is a rare instance of a witness documenting his own falsification and the motive for it.

The formula Shen Zui says he used in class in place of the real reason. He is explicit that he knew it to be false at the time. Read with the confession-and-reform framing this book was published under, the admission does double work: it condemns the earlier lie and authenticates the present account.

上海独立运动. Shi Liangcai chaired the Shanghai municipal council, and a movement to take the city out from under Nationalist rule was the pretext Dai Li gave the operations group. Shen Zui reports the pretext and the truth separately, which is the chapter's method throughout.

中统, the Nationalist party's rival intelligence service, run through the CC Clique of the Chen brothers. Shen Zui's reasoning here is worth noting as organizational evidence: he argues the killing must have been Communist-related because a merely anti-Chiang newspaper would have been the Zhongtong's business, and Dai Li, at odds with them throughout, would never have done their work.

The faction of Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, which controlled the Nationalist party apparatus and the Zhongtong. The Juntong-Zhongtong rivalry runs through the whole book and is here used as a piece of deduction about who ordered what.

The Juntong operative serving as a Chinese detective inspector in the French concession police, through whom, in Shen Zui's account, the poison reached Guo Decheng. The placing of the Juntong's own men inside the concession forces is the structural point: the organization could reach a prisoner in foreign custody.
广慈医院 on Route Pere Robert, the French Catholic hospital, now Ruijin Hospital, where Yang Xingfo was taken and died and where the wounded gunman was treated.

The name Peking carried from 1928 to 1949, when the capital was at Nanking: 北平, 'northern peace', rather than 北京, 'northern capital'. Yang Xingfo's northern tour in the spring of 1933, and the League's work there, immediately preceded the decision to kill him.

ch02.anchor: Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party
ch02.note: The Party's central organs were based in Shanghai from 1921 until the leadership moved to the Kiangsi soviet in 1933, working underground in the foreign concessions where Chinese police powers did not reach. That is the fact the whole chapter rests on: the Juntong's Shanghai work existed because the Party's did.
特务处 of the Renaissance Society, the Blue Shirts, founded 1932 and the direct ancestor of the Juntong. Shen Zui joined it that year as a courier for the East China district, aged eighteen.

The Shanghai International Settlement and the French Concession were separately administered and had their own police forces, so that Chinese government agents operated there without jurisdiction. The chapter turns on this repeatedly: killings staged inside the concessions to demonstrate reach, prisoners handed over by concession police, and Juntong men holding posts within those forces.
The Huangpu river. Shen Zui's account of bodies weighted and dropped into it is given without qualification and he names himself present at some of the disposals.

化骨水. Shen Zui says he saw a body destroyed with it once, in 1933 or 1934. The substance is presumably a strong acid; he does not identify it and shows no interest in what it was. The passage is among the flattest in the book and the flatness is the point.

Zhao Lijun (1905-1942), head of the East China district's operations group and the Juntong's principal assassin in Shanghai, responsible for both the Yang Xingfo and Shi Liangcai killings. He was executed by the Nationalist government itself in 1942 after murdering a county magistrate in Honan. Shen Zui worked under him and is the chief source for both cases.

Head of the Juntong's Shanghai district for much of this period. The OCR mangled his name six separate ways across this chapter, every one of them a plausible-looking word; the readings here are crop-verified against the scan.
A Shanghai district colleague who appears throughout Shen Zui's account of these years, including in the episodes where he himself was punished.

Cui Wanqiu (1903-1990), journalist, editor of the literary supplement *Torch* of the *Great Evening News*. The passage naming him is the most historically loaded in the chapter and is set out in the notes that follow.

Zhang Chunqiao (1917-2005), later a member of the Politburo Standing Committee and of the Gang of Four, tried and condemned in 1981. Shen Zui states that in his Shanghai years Zhang wrote under the pen name Di Ke and attacked Lu Xun in print. That Zhang used the name Di Ke and published a piece critical of Lu Xun in 1936 is documented and was made much of during his trial. Shen Zui was writing after Zhang's fall, when saying so carried no risk and some advantage, and the passage should be read with that in mind. The reading here is crop-verified against the scan rather than trusted to OCR, precisely because of what it asserts.

The stage name of Jiang Qing (1914-1991), Mao Zedong's wife and, like Zhang Chunqiao, condemned as one of the Gang of Four. She acted in Shanghai under that name in the mid-1930s. Shen Zui places her at Cui Wanqiu's house. Like the Zhang Chunqiao material, this was written after her fall; it is the single most politically charged sentence in the chapter and it is impossible to separate what he knew from what it was safe and useful to say in the early 1960s and after. Crop-verified as printed.
Lu Xun (1881-1936), the foremost modern Chinese writer, living in Shanghai through these years and a target of Nationalist surveillance himself.
Zou Taofen (1895-1944), journalist and publisher, editor of *Life Weekly*, one of the Seven Gentlemen arrested in 1936. He appears here as a person the Juntong watched.

Che Yaoxian (1894-1940), a Communist working under cover in Szechwan, arrested and killed by the Nationalists. His appearance in this chapter is one of the places where Shen Zui's account intersects a documented case.

Song Qingling (1893-1981), Sun Yat-sen's widow. The surveillance section describes years of unbroken watch on her at Chiang Kai-shek's personal direction, and then the scheme Shen Zui himself devised: to ram her car with another and injure her badly enough to stop her activity. He reports that he put it to Dai Li, that Dai Li thought well of it, and that it awaited Chiang Kai-shek's approval. Nothing came of it. It is the most self-incriminating passage in the chapter and he sets it down without mitigation.
Du Yuesheng (1888-1951), head of the Green Gang and the dominant power in the Shanghai underworld, whose relations with the Nationalist security services were close throughout.
青帮, the secret society that controlled much of Shanghai's opium traffic, labour and protection rackets, and which the Nationalists had used against the Communists since the massacre of 1927.

Yang Hu (1889-1966), Shanghai garrison commander, one of the men who carried out the 1927 purge of Communists in the city. Shen Zui's point in naming him is jurisdictional: even a garrison commander hand in glove with Dai Li could not interfere in the district's work.

淞沪警备司令部, the Chinese military authority for the Shanghai area, with powers of arrest and military trial over Chinese territory outside the concessions. Political prisoners taken by the Juntong were commonly passed to it or to Nanking.

龙泉驿 outside Chengtu, site of the Juntong's own cemetery. Dai Li's visits to a subordinate's grave there, and his weeping, are given by Shen Zui as evidence of the personal hold he kept over the organization; the chapter elsewhere shows what that loyalty was worth when an operation needed protecting.

The foreign instructor whose real name Shen Zui says he learned only after liberation, from material provided by others. The Juntong's employment of foreign technical instructors before the war is plausible and lightly documented; this identification rests on post-1949 sources Shen Zui does not name and cannot be checked here.

叛徒, the standard term for a Party member who turned. The chapter's central figure in this line is Lu Haifang, whose defection Shen Zui describes at length, including the identification that led to an arrest in the street. The word carries in Chinese a weight closer to 'traitor' than the English 'renegade' conveys.

The Communist who turned and then worked for the Juntong identifying former comrades. Shen Zui's remark that he had never seen anyone turn faster is one of several places where the narrator's professional appraisal and the moral judgement required of the book sit uneasily together.
The Whampoa Military Academy near Canton, founded 1924 with Chiang Kai-shek as commandant. Intake numbers functioned throughout the Nationalist services as markers of seniority and patronage.
Suzhou, site of the model prison where political prisoners from the Shanghai region were held, and where Chen Duxiu was imprisoned from 1932.
Hangzhou. The Shanghai-Hangchow road is where Shi Liangcai was killed, and the route appears throughout as the corridor between the two cities.
虹口, the northern Shanghai district with the largest Japanese population, effectively under Japanese influence before the war.
闸北, the Chinese-administered district north of the Settlement, heavily damaged in the fighting of 1932 and again in 1937.
Chengdu, capital of Szechwan.

Nanjing, the Nationalist capital from 1927 to 1937. Political prisoners of consequence were sent there from Shanghai, and the chapter's section on escorting prisoners describes the methods used on that route.

Personal direction from Chiang Kai-shek appears repeatedly in this chapter -- the standing surveillance of Song Qingling, the insistence that Yang Xingfo be killed inside the French Concession, the approval awaited for the scheme against Song Qingling's car. Shen Zui presents the Juntong throughout as executing instructions rather than initiating, which is both plausible for its structure and convenient for a memoirist.

反动派. The standard designation in mainland writing of the period for the Nationalists, used here by a former Nationalist officer of his own former service. Preserved rather than neutralized: the vocabulary is evidence of the conditions the book was written under.

The section title is 我受到的惩罚. Shen Zui devotes it to his own disciplinary punishments within the Juntong -- for taking a prisoner's possessions, among other things -- and draws from them the lesson he says he afterwards taught his students. The confessional frame and the professional lesson are delivered in the same breath, which is characteristic of the book.

酷刑种种. The section catalogues the methods in the plain enumerative register the whole chapter uses. Shen Zui taught this material; the later Chungking chapter has him contributing to the design of new instruments and testing them. Nothing here is presented as exceptional or as exceeding orders.

绑票, literally 'binding a ticket', the ordinary Chinese word for kidnapping for ransom, applied without irony to political abduction. Shen Zui records Dai Li encouraging the group to develop methods that would work in a crowded street in broad daylight rather than only in quiet districts.

监视工作. The final section, and the one that names Song Qingling. It is also where Shen Zui records the limits: agents telephoned and wrote to intimidate her, a plot to sabotage her car was forbidden by Dai Li, and the anonymous letters and calls were allowed to continue.
Deputy head of the East China district's operations group under Zhao Lijun, named in the account of the Yang Xingfo killing in the following chapter as well.

One of the figures Shen Zui names in the Shanghai district's dealings. The reading is crop-verified; the man is not otherwise identifiable from the sources available here and the romanization is provisional.
Named in the Shanghai narrative; the reading is crop-verified against the scan. Not otherwise identifiable here, and the romanization is provisional.

军统, short for 国民政府军事委员会调查统计局, the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission. Strictly the name dates only from 1938, and Shen Zui applies it throughout to the pre-war Special Services Department as well, as the book's own usage does.

交通, the district's runner, carrying messages and material between cells that were not permitted to know one another. It was Shen Zui's first post in the organization, at eighteen, and it is why he was present at so much of what this chapter describes without having ordered any of it.

情报组 and 行动组, the intelligence and operations groups, were the two halves of a Juntong district: one gathered, the other seized and killed. Shen Zui held posts in both, which is unusual and is the reason his account covers the whole cycle from surveillance to disposal.

华东区, the Juntong's regional organization covering Shanghai and the lower Yangtze, later reorganized as the Shanghai special district. The name changes during the period this chapter covers, which is why Shen Zui explains his own postings twice.

地下, of Party organization operating in secret. The word is used throughout for what the Juntong was hunting, and the chapter's structure follows the hunt: find the cell, take one member, turn him, use him to identify the rest.

The concession police forces employed Chinese detectives under foreign command, and the Juntong placed its own men among them. That is how, in the following chapter, poison reaches a prisoner in French custody. The arrangement is the practical answer to the jurisdictional problem the concessions posed.
